title: Mount Horeb Earthworks
summary: Above Elkhorn Creek near Lexington, the Mount Horeb Earthworks are a circular ditch-and-embankment enclosure built by Adena people, now in Adena Park.
bodyMarkdown:
Around two thousand years ago, people of the [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) shaped a bluff above Elkhorn Creek, in what is now Fayette County, into a ceremonial landscape. They did not build a fort or a village there. Instead they built circles, a design that still puzzles and impresses archaeologists.

The site sits on a bank about 75 feet above the creek. The centerpiece of the [Mount Horeb Earthworks Complex](https://grokipedia.com/page/mount_horeb_earthworks_complex) is a causewayed ring ditch. A circular platform about 105 feet across is surrounded by a ditch about 45 feet wide and an outer embankment about 13 feet wide, with an entry about 33 feet wide on the west. The layout, with the ditch inside the embankment, does not look like a defensive work.

Excavation revealed more than earth. In 1939, archaeologist William S. Webb and crews hired through the [Works Progress Administration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Works_Progress_Administration) found the post pattern of a circular timber structure about 48.5 feet across, built of 132 posts, 62 of them set in pairs. Researchers date the Adena tradition to roughly 600 BCE to the first centuries CE. Webb speculated that the structure was a ceremonial center for a nearby clan.

The bluff was part of a larger Adena landscape. The complex includes other earthworks along the creek, among them the large enclosure known as [Peter Village](/stories/peter-village-enclosure-15fa166/). During the [Woodland period](https://grokipedia.com/page/Woodland_period), Adena people lived in small, dispersed communities, typically along river terraces and valley rims, much like this bluff above the Elkhorn. Mount Horeb is one of several Adena sites in Kentucky's Bluegrass region, and others are found across the state (see [Ashland's Adena Mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/)).

The site survived because people chose to protect it. In 1936 private donors bought about six acres for the Kentucky Archaeological Society, and the land later passed to the University of Kentucky. That early purchase is why the ring can still be seen today.

## Kentucky today

The Mount Horeb earthwork is the centerpiece of the University of Kentucky's Adena Park, which the university owns and operates through its Campus Recreation Department, according to [an article on the Mount Horeb Earthworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Horeb_Earthworks_Complex). The ring still sits on the bluff above Elkhorn Creek, where Adena builders first shaped it.
